title: Specimen Numbers: Heel Sticks, 24-Hour Urine and Spin Math
summary: Work the Ch. 3 number vault: safe heel-puncture depth, the 24-hour urine “toilet first, jug last” rule and its preservatives, rpm-to-g conversion — and which figures the sources disagree on.

reviewer.note: Completes the Ch. 3 Number Vault table. Rows already taught elsewhere: citrate 9 : 1, catheter discard, clot times, blood-gas heparin, fluoride timing, EDTA K⁺, urine 1-hour rule, WBIT rates. This lesson teaches the rest; rows not matched to a source (ESR 4 : 1, vacuum volumes, K3EDTA dilution, 42 °C warming, CSF pressures, centrifugation 850–1,000 g, creatinine rise, trough timing, boric acid, 4-L container, creatinine completeness, formaldehyde SG) are taught as pending reviewer figures.

objectives: Choose a safe heel-puncture site and depth.
Collect a 24-hour urine correctly and match common preservatives to tests.
Convert rpm to relative centrifugal force and explain why doubling rpm quadruples g.
Recognize specimen numbers on which sources disagree, and defer to lab policy.

scenes.title: The specimen number vault
scenes.altText: A vault door swings open and number chips tumble out: 9 : 1, 4 : 1, 2.4 mm, 10 min, 1,000 g, 24 h, 6N HCl. The cartoon scientist catches them with a clipboard labelled “Which ones are rules, and which still need checking?”

cues.text: Specimen collection is full of numbers: ratios, depths, speeds, times.
Some come straight from guidelines. Some are the reviewer’s figures that we have not been able to confirm yet.
Let’s learn the most useful ones by working with them — and keep track of which are checked.

props.label: Rules vs figures still to check

scenes.title: Skin punctures and tube ratios
scenes.altText: A baby’s heel outline with three zones: medial and lateral plantar heel (about 3.3 mm to bone, safe zones) and the posterior heel (about 2.3 mm to bone, avoid). A lancet bar shows WHO’s limit of 2.4 mm depth; the reviewer’s 2 mm figure sits beside it. Then ratio chips: light-blue coag tube 9 : 1, black ESR tube 4 : 1 (reviewer), liquid K3EDTA diluting the sample 1–2% (reviewer), and evacuated tube volumes set by their vacuum.

cues.text: Heel sticks are for babies. WHO gives the distance from skin to bone in a 3-kilogram baby: about 3.3 millimetres at the sides of the heel, but only about 2.3 at the back.
So puncture the medial or lateral side, avoid the back of the heel, and keep the depth under 2.4 millimetres. The reviewer gives 2 millimetres — a stricter figure.
Warming the site with a warm cloth increases blood flow. The reviewer limits the temperature to 42 degrees Celsius.
Tube ratios: the light-blue coag tube is 9 parts blood to 1 part citrate. The reviewer adds that the black ESR tube uses 4 to 1.
The reviewer also notes that evacuated tubes draw a set volume because of their vacuum, and that liquid K3 EDTA dilutes the sample by 1 to 2 percent, while spray-dried K2 EDTA does not.

props.label: Liquid K3EDTA dilutes 1–2% · spray-dried K2EDTA doesn’t (reviewer)

scenes.title: The 24-hour urine
scenes.altText: A 24-hour clock. At 7 am the first void goes to the toilet (crossed out — not collected). Every void after that drops into a big jug in a fridge (2–8 °C). At 7 am the next day the final void goes INTO the jug. Preservative chips attach to the jug: 6N HCl (catecholamines, calcium, oxalate, magnesium, phosphorus, citrate, cystine), acetic acid (ALA, porphobilinogen), sodium fluoride (glucose), sodium carbonate (porphyrins).

cues.text: Some tests need all the urine made in a whole day. Day one, 7 am: empty the bladder into the toilet. That urine was made before the clock started, so it is not collected.
From then on, every drop goes into the container, kept refrigerated or cool.
Day two, 7 am: empty the bladder one last time — and this time it goes INTO the container. It was made during the 24 hours.
Many collections need a preservative in the jug. Hydrochloric acid, 6 normal, is used for catecholamines, calcium, oxalate and several others. Sodium fluoride protects glucose.
The reviewer adds that boric acid is used for aldosterone and cortisol, and that urine creatinine helps show whether the collection was complete.

props.label: Reviewer: boric acid (aldosterone, cortisol) · creatinine checks completeness

scenes.title: In the lab: spin math
scenes.altText: A centrifuge rotor with radius r = 10 cm spins at 3,000 rpm. The formula RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × rpm² fills in: 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × 10 × 9,000,000 ≈ 1,006 × g. A second line doubles the speed to 6,000 rpm and the force quadruples to about 4,025 × g. A plasma-spin card: about 850–1,000 × g for 10 minutes within 1 hour of collection (reviewer).

cues.text: Centrifuges are set in rpm, but procedures are written in g — the force on the tube. You convert with the RCF formula.
RCF equals 1.118 times ten to the minus five, times the radius in centimetres, times the rpm squared.
Example: radius 10 centimetres at 3,000 rpm. 3,000 squared is 9 million. Times 10, times 1.118 times ten to the minus five: about 1,006 g.
Because rpm is squared, doubling the speed to 6,000 rpm makes the force four times larger — about 4,025 g.
The reviewer’s plasma rule: spin at about 850 to 1,000 g for 10 minutes, within an hour of collection, with the tube stoppered.

props.title: RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × rpm²
lines: r in cm, from axis to tube bottom

scenes.title: Numbers the sources disagree on
scenes.altText: Three cards. “Arterial blood gas transport”: WHO 2010 puts the syringe in an ice cup; Sood 2010 says do not cool and analyse within 30 minutes; the reviewer gives 1–5 °C ice water → follow the lab’s policy for its syringe type. “Heel depth”: WHO ≤ 2.4 mm vs reviewer ≤ 2 mm. “Other reviewer figures (unverified)”: CSF opening pressure 90–180 mmH₂O; remove ≤ 2 mL if > 200; trough 30 min before dose; unseparated creatinine rises; formaldehyde tablet +0.002 SG.

cues.text: Some numbers depend on the source. Blood-gas transport: WHO places the syringe in an ice cup, but another review says do not cool and test within 30 minutes. Follow your lab’s policy for its syringe type.
Heel depth: WHO says no deeper than 2.4 millimetres; the reviewer says 2. On an exam, know both and avoid the back of the heel.

And a set of reviewer figures we have not verified yet: CSF opening pressure 90 to 180 millimetres of water; remove no more than 2 millilitres if it is over 200; troughs drawn 30 minutes before a dose; creatinine rising in unseparated blood; and formaldehyde tablets raising specific gravity.

Reviewer: 1–5 °C ice water → follow lab policy

props.title: Heel depth: WHO ≤ 2.4 mm · reviewer ≤ 2 mm

scenes.title: Double the speed, four times the g
scenes.altText: Memory aid: a centrifuge with “×2 speed” and a weight showing “×4 g”. Beside it, a clock reading “Toilet first, jug last” for the 24-hour urine. A card lists where the aid breaks down.

cues.text: Memory aid: double the speed, four times the g — because rpm is squared.
And for 24-hour urine: toilet first, jug last.
Where it breaks: g also depends on the radius, so the same rpm gives different g in different centrifuges. And preservatives depend on the test — always check the lab’s list.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × rpm²”, “24-h urine: toilet first, jug last”, “Heel: sides, ≤ 2.4 mm (WHO)”.

cues.text: Convert rpm to g with RCF equals 1.118 times ten to the minus five times radius times rpm squared, collect 24-hour urine by discarding the first void and keeping the last, and puncture heels at the sides no deeper than WHO’s 2.4 millimetres — checking each remaining number against your lab’s procedure.

explanation.what: Plain language: specimen collection uses many set numbers — how deep to prick a baby’s heel, how to time a full day’s urine, and how hard to spin a tube. Scientific terms: WHO limits heel-puncture depth to 2.4 mm and advises avoiding the posterior heel; a 24-hour urine discards the first void and includes the final void 24 hours later, refrigerated, often with a test-specific preservative; RCF (× g) = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r (cm) × rpm².
explanation.why: In a 3-kg baby the bone is about 3.3 mm under the medial and lateral heel but only about 2.3 mm under the posterior heel, so depth and site prevent bone injury. The first morning void was made before the collection window; the final void was made within it. Centrifugal force rises with the square of speed and in proportion to radius.
explanation.measure: Labs set centrifuges from RCF (e.g., r 10 cm at 3,000 rpm ≈ 1,006 × g), check 24-hour volumes and preservatives, and reject collections that are incomplete or wrongly preserved.
explanation.differs: First void (discard) vs final void (keep). rpm (machine setting) vs g (force on the sample). Sources differ on blood-gas cooling (WHO ice cup vs Sood “do not cool”) and heel depth (WHO 2.4 mm vs reviewer 2 mm).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: an RCF calculation, the 24-hour urine steps, which preservative for catecholamines (HCl) or glucose (NaF), the safe heel site and depth, and the 9 : 1 vs 4 : 1 citrate ratios.

mnemonic.text: Double the speed, four times the g — and toilet first, jug last.
mnemonic.explanation: rpm is squared in the RCF formula; the first void of a 24-hour urine is discarded and the final void is kept.
mnemonic.limitation: g also depends on the rotor radius, so the same rpm gives different g in different centrifuges. Preservatives depend on the test and the lab’s procedure. The aid says nothing about heel sticks or which reviewer numbers remain unverified.

takeaway: Convert rpm to g with RCF equals 1.118 times ten to the minus five times radius times rpm squared, collect 24-hour urine by discarding the first void and keeping the last, and puncture heels at the sides no deeper than WHO’s 2.4 millimetres — checking each remaining number against your lab’s procedure.

questions.stem: A centrifuge has a radius of 15 cm and runs at 2,000 rpm. What is the RCF? (RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × rpm²)

options.rationale: Incorrect. This uses 1,000 rpm instead of 2,000 (1,000² × 15 × 1.118 × 10⁻⁵).
Incorrect. This uses 4,000 rpm — double the actual speed.
Incorrect. This forgets to square the rpm (1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × 15 × 2,000).

questions.stem: How should a patient start and finish a 24-hour urine collection that begins at 7 am Monday?

options.text: Void into the toilet at 7 am Monday, collect all urine after that, and add the 7 am Tuesday void to the container
options.rationale: Correct. The first void was made before the window; the final void was made within it.

options.text: Collect the 7 am Monday void and discard the 7 am Tuesday void
options.rationale: Incorrect. This reverses the rule and shifts the window.

options.text: Collect only daytime urine and skip the night
options.rationale: Incorrect. All urine for 24 hours, day and night, must be collected.

options.text: Keep the container at room temperature without any preservative for all tests
options.rationale: Incorrect. Collections are kept cool and may need a test-specific preservative.

questions.stem: Which heel-puncture practice for a newborn follows WHO guidance?

options.text: Puncture the medial or lateral heel with a depth no greater than 2.4 mm, avoiding the posterior heel
options.rationale: Correct. Bone lies only about 2.3 mm under the posterior heel; the sides allow a safe shallow puncture.

options.text: Puncture the posterior curvature of the heel with a 3 mm lancet
options.rationale: Incorrect. The posterior heel is closest to bone; 3 mm exceeds the depth limit.

options.text: Use the deepest lancet available to get more blood
options.rationale: Incorrect. Depth must be limited to avoid bone injury and infection.

options.text: Puncture the same spot repeatedly to save time
options.rationale: Incorrect. Repeated punctures at one site raise injury and infection risk.

claims.text: Heel-prick depth ≤ 2.4 mm; avoid the posterior heel (≈ 2.33 mm to bone vs ≈ 3.32 mm medial/lateral in a 3-kg baby).

24-hour urine: discard the first void, collect for 24 h including the final void, refrigerate; HCl for catecholamines and others, acetic acid for ALA/PBG, NaF for glucose, sodium carbonate for porphyrins.
RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × rpm²; worked examples: r 10 cm, 3,000 rpm ≈ 1,006 g; 6,000 rpm ≈ 4,025 g; r 15 cm, 2,000 rpm ≈ 671 g.
claims.note: Examples are arithmetic with the cited formula.

claims.text: Sources differ on cooling arterial blood-gas samples: WHO 2010 uses an ice cup; Sood 2010 says do not cool and analyse within 30 min.

Reviewer figures: heel ≤ 2 mm; skin warming ≤ 42 °C; ESR citrate 4 : 1; vacuum sets draw volume (3.5, 4.0, 4.5, 8.5 mL); liquid K3EDTA dilutes 1–2%; arterial transport 1–5 °C ice water; compression ≥ 3–5 min; CSF opening pressure 90–180 mmH₂O and ≤ 2 mL removal if > 200; plasma spin 850–1,000 g × 10 min within 1 h; unseparated creatinine rise; trough 30 min before dose; boric acid 10 g (aldosterone, cortisol), 6N HCl 10 mL, NaF 0.5 g; ~4-L container, 40-mL aliquot, creatinine for completeness; formaldehyde tablet +0.002 SG.
